definitions.explanation: A traditional Japanese sliding door made of a wooden lattice frame covered with translucent washi paper. Used as room dividers and exterior doors in traditional Japanese architecture.

examples.japanese: {障子戸|しょうじど}を{開|あ}けると{庭|にわ}が{見|み}えた。
examples.english: When I opened the shoji door, I could see the garden.

examples.japanese: {子供|こども}が{障子戸|しょうじど}の{紙|かみ}に{穴|あな}を{開|あ}けてしまった。
examples.english: The child poked a hole in the shoji door's paper.

examples.japanese: {古|ふる}い{旅館|りょかん}の{障子戸|しょうじど}から{柔|やわ}らかい{光|ひかり}が{差|さ}し{込|こ}んでいた。
examples.english: Soft light was streaming in through the shoji doors of the old inn.

notes:
A compound of {障子|しょうじ} (shoji screen) and {戸|ど} (door). While {障子|しょうじ} alone often refers to the same thing, {障子戸|しょうじど} specifically emphasizes its function as a door (opening/closing to enter/exit). The translucent paper allows soft, diffused light to pass through while providing privacy.

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {障子戸|しょうじど}を{開|あ}ける — to open the shoji door
- {障子戸|しょうじど}を{閉|し}める — to close the shoji door
- {障子戸|しょうじど}の{張|は}り{替|か}え — re-papering of shoji doors

CULTURAL NOTE:
Shoji doors are a defining feature of traditional Japanese houses ({和室|わしつ}). The paper is typically replaced annually, often at year-end cleaning ({大掃除|おおそうじ}). In modern homes, glass or acrylic panels sometimes replace the traditional {和紙|わし}.

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {障子|しょうじ} — shoji (the screen/panel itself, often used interchangeably)
- {襖|ふすま} — fusuma (opaque sliding door, thicker and painted, used between rooms)
- {引|ひ}き{戸|ど} — sliding door (general term for any sliding door)
